1.pericope_label: Pharaoh dreams of the kine and the ears

schools.summary: Gill leaves the two years' reckoning open but prefers dating them from the butler's release, since that connects this chapter with the last, and describes the kine as rising from the river because they were fed by what the Nile's overflow produced. Calvin reads years of days as complete years and treats the delay as a second trial in which every human ground of hope was withdrawn; he then presses the doctrine that God will sometimes grant his oracles to profane men, though the doctrine of eternal life belongs to the Church alone, and explains the doubled dream as his ordinary method of repeating and clarifying.

Henry makes the delay the lesson: we need patience not only to bear but to wait, a time is set for the deliverance of God's people, and two full years is not too long to continue waiting. He notes that the magicians' failure was allowed so that Joseph's performance by the Spirit of God might appear the more admirable, human prudence being nonplussed that divine revelation may be the more glorious.

Clarke reads two years of days as two complete solar revolutions and identifies the river as the Nile, the cause of Egypt's fertility. He insists the kine must be the hippopotamus, since only that animal comes up out of the river to feed in the field, and gives a long account of the east wind's destructiveness in Egypt, including a traveller's narrative of the simoom near Syene.

Ellicott explains the Egyptian detail throughout: the river is Yeor, the Egyptian word for great river; the cow was the symbol of earth and agriculture and the cows of Isis were seven; the meadow is marsh-grass of the Nile banks; and the ears on one stalk are the Egyptian wheat that bears several heads on one stem. On the wind he is cautious, suggesting the south-eastern Chamsin. Keil and Delitzsch note only that the vision was so like reality that Pharaoh knew it for a dream only on waking.

debates: From what point the two years are counted. Gill weighs imprisonment against the butler's release and prefers the latter; Clarke simply dates them from the events of the preceding chapter.

What the kine are. Clarke argues from their coming out of the water and feeding in the field that they must be the hippopotamus; Ellicott keeps them cattle and explains them as the Egyptian symbol of the earth.

Which wind is meant. Clarke takes the east wind straightforwardly and describes its Egyptian violence; Ellicott suggests the south-eastern Chamsin, since Hebrew has words only for the four chief winds.
outliers: Clarke's extended traveller's account of the simoom, with the purple haze twelve feet high and the company lying flat as dead, is far longer than anything else offered on the verse.
Ellicott overturns the classical claim that Egyptians despised wheat by appealing to the temple paintings of the Theban district.
themes: the Nile as the whole source of fertility

8.pericope_label: The magicians fail and the butler remembers Joseph

schools.summary: Gill has the dream standing before Pharaoh awake as it had asleep, so that the king could have no ease until he knew its meaning. Calvin treats the king's anxiety as an inward seal authenticating the dream, condemns his running to magicians as a voluntary closing of the eyes that excuses nothing, and takes their being struck dumb for a mercy, since God provides best when he removes the incitements of error; the whole providence, he insists, was aimed not at Egypt but at bringing Joseph out and feeding the Church, which God esteems above ten worlds.

Henry judges the butler's confession more a compliment to Pharaoh than gratitude to Joseph, yet grants that remembering one's faults and repenting late is better than never. He makes the two years' delay providential: an earlier release would probably have sent Joseph home to the land of the Hebrews, and those who wait for God are paid principal and interest.

Clarke thinks the word for the magicians is Egyptian and its etymology lost with the art of hieroglyphs, though he reports the Hebrew derivation from a pen and a verb to perfect, and gives a glowing classical account of the wise men, among whom Pythagoras is said to have conversed and from whom he took the name philosopher. On the butler he is severe: the man could not have forgotten, only found it inconvenient to remember until it served his interest. Wesley notes that the rules of the magicians' art failed them, which made Joseph's performance by the Spirit the more admirable.

Keil and Delitzsch derive the title from a stylus and identify these men with the sacred scribes of the priestly caste, keepers of hieroglyphics, astrology, dream interpretation and magic, and find their failure ironical since the clue lay in Egypt's own symbols, the cow standing for earth and food and the Nile for fertility. Ellicott adds that their real knowledge was habitually dressed in a claim to occult acquaintance with the secrets of the gods, sustained by popular superstition, and supposes several did attempt the dream but too imperfectly to satisfy the king.

debates: What the magicians were. Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott settle on the sacred scribes of the priestly caste; Clarke doubts the word is Hebrew at all and leaves its etymology unknown.

What the butler's confessed faults were. Henry and Wesley take them for his neglect of Joseph, while noting that some read them as his old offence against Pharaoh; Calvin insists on the latter, as a courtier's necessary preface rather than any repentance.
Why no interpretation was offered. Ellicott thinks attempts were made and simply failed to satisfy; Calvin holds that God struck the soothsayers dumb so that no plausible answer could be found.
outliers: Clarke traces the word philosopher to Pythagoras' contact with the Egyptian wise men, a derivation nobody else raises.
Calvin values the Church above ten worlds and makes the entire Egyptian famine policy subordinate to feeding it.
themes: God removes the means of self-deception

14.pericope_label: Joseph is fetched from the dungeon and disclaims the gift

schools.summary: Gill has Pharaoh order the prisoner loosed at once and hears in Joseph's disclaimer great modesty, a refusal to arrogate skill that was purely a gift of God. Calvin reads the summons as a lesson in what necessity can effect on a proud king, and applies it to the elect, who become docile only when the pride of the flesh is laid low; he takes the shaving and change of raiment as the removal of prison filth, and treats Joseph's answer as a total renunciation of personal honour, with the promised peace a prayer rather than a prophecy since the oracle was not yet known.

Clarke thinks the beard was trimmed rather than shaved in our sense and that the fresh clothing must have come from the royal wardrobe, and renders the disclaimer as without me, independently of me — Joseph telling the king he is not essential to his comfort, since God has him under his care, and pointing him to the source of all prosperity. Wesley draws out the two courtesies of the answer, honour given to God and good-will shown to Pharaoh, and adds that those who consult God's oracles may expect an answer of peace.

Ellicott documents the Egyptian custom from Herodotus and the monuments, where beards mark captives and men of low condition and the hair is grown only in mourning, so that Joseph's shaving is exactly what a summons to court required. He also passes on Abravanel's tally of exact recompenses, dreams for dreams, fine linen for the stripped coat, the pit of the prison for the pit at Dothan, and lordship for slavery.

debates: Whether Egyptians wore their hair long. Calvin conjectures that so elegant a nation would rather have nourished it; Ellicott shows from the classical writers and the sculptures that the reverse was true and a beard was a mark of disgrace.
What the promised peace amounts to. Calvin makes it a prayer offered before Joseph knew the oracle; Clarke and Wesley take it as a genuine assurance of prosperity that conciliated the king.
outliers: Abravanel's list of exact recompenses, reported by Ellicott, matches each of Joseph's sufferings to its reversal.
Calvin's remark that the servant of God lay in filth to the very day of his deliverance is bleaker than anything else said of the imprisonment.

17.pericope_label: Pharaoh repeats the dream in his own words

schools.summary: Gill notes the recital is fuller than the first telling and gathers the rabbinic readings of the unique word for the withered ears — small, empty husk, mere images of ears, or dry as a rock. Calvin takes the detail that the lean kine were nothing better for their meal as God's testimony that the people would be famished even amid gathered stores, and builds on Joseph's phrasing a full argument that God foretells only what he himself has determined to do, so that providence cannot be separated from eternal counsel and continual operation.

Henry explains the whole from the river: Egypt has no rain, and fifteen or sixteen cubits of inundation meant plenty while twelve or thirteen meant scarcity, yet the dependence is on the first Cause and not the second. He makes the doubling mark certainty, nearness and importance, while the two figures answer to grass and corn, and draws the practical lessons that the comforts of life are subject to change and that magistrates, being shepherds, must feed as well as rule.

Clarke observes that both sets of kine rose from the same river, which shows at once the cause of the plenty and of the dearth, since fertility is proportioned to the inundation. On the lean cattle gaining nothing by their meal he offers a physiological account, that want sharpens appetite and hurries food through the body before its nourishment can be taken up, and calls the description physically correct.

Ellicott documents the differences between the dream as narrated and as recited, the king adding his own impressions of cattle worse than any he had seen and unchanged after eating, with the terms for them slightly rearranged. He renders the unique word for the bad ears as stony, the grains shrivelled and hard like bits of grit, and repeats that the meadow is properly marsh-grass.

debates: What the unique word for the withered ears means. Gill reports rabbinic readings of small, empty, mere images, and rock-dry; Ellicott settles on stony, that is shrivelled and gritty.

Whether divine foreknowledge implies divine determination. Calvin argues at length against those who allow God prescience while denying that it involves the event, insisting God foreknows because he has decreed.
Why the lean kine gained nothing. Clarke explains it physiologically from the effect of hunger on digestion; Calvin takes it as a sign that stored abundance would not save the people.
outliers: Clarke's account of accelerated digestion under famine is unlike anything else offered on the chapter.
Henry turns the revelation to Pharaoh into a charge on magistrates, who as shepherds must feed and not only rule.
themes: second causes and the first Cause

25.pericope_label: Joseph interprets the seven years of plenty and famine

schools.summary: Gill reads the two dreams as one in sense, gives the plenty as abundance to the point of luxury when the Nile reached sixteen cubits and the famine as its failure at twelve, and insists that seven successive years either way can be ascribed only to God; he notes too that the plenty remained known while the stores lasted but left no trace by the end. Calvin explains the doubling as no sign of mutability but a concession to human dullness, since God speaks from a fixed purpose and once would suffice, and adds that the nearness of the event is pressed so the king should not slumber in expectation of delay.

Clarke argues that the dreams were sent to show that even the inundation, the ordinary cause of plenty and want, lies under an overruling providence, and reproduces the ancient scale of the Nile in full — twelve cubits famine, thirteen hunger, fourteen rejoicing, fifteen security, sixteen luxury, with eighteen ruinous because seed-time is lost. Wesley finds mercy in the order of the years, plenty sent first that provision might be made, and sets against it the perishing nature of worldly enjoyments, since the whole surplus did but keep men alive.

debates: How precisely the river's height governs the harvest. Gill cites sixteen cubits for abundance and twelve for famine; Clarke gives the entire graduated scale and adds that too high a flood is as fatal as too low.
What the repetition of the dream signifies. Calvin denies it implies any instability in the decree and refers it wholly to our weakness of memory and confidence.
outliers: Clarke's claim that eighteen cubits produces famine as surely as a failed inundation reverses the usual assumption that more water is better.
Wesley applies the manna rule, that he who gathered much had nothing over, to the ordinary course of harvests.
themes: the decree is fixed and near

33.pericope_label: Joseph advises a discreet man, officers, and a fifth part

schools.summary: Gill denies that Joseph had himself in view, holding it inconsistent with his modesty and noting that he offered no advice until asked, and takes the stores to be deposits in the cities against public distress. Calvin treats the unasked counsel as proof of the prophetic office, since true prophets propose remedies and not bare predictions, contrasts this with pagan oracles that produce only presumption or despair, and explains the royal granaries as a necessary bridle on the intemperance of prosperous men, which would also teach the people frugality.

Henry makes the advice a pattern of prudence — fair warning followed by good counsel, times of gathering improved against a time of spending, the ant's example — and sees administrative sense in appointing officers and one man over them, since what is everybody's business proves nobody's. He observes that Pharaoh's counsellors could no more improve the dream than the magicians could interpret it, so that Joseph taught the senators wisdom.

Clarke reasons that since Joseph could not have foreseen his own elevation the counsel was disinterested, and was either directly inspired or simply sound policy. He renders the officers as visitors or overseers, reports Ainsworth's rendering of bishops, and argues that although the customary levy was probably a tenth, the extraordinary harvest made a fifth reasonable and not oppressive.

Ellicott reads the Hebrew as let him fifth the land, agrees that a tithe was likely the standing impost and that doubling it would not press hard in years of such plenty, and notes that publishing the reason would prompt careful people to store their own surplus too. He adds that a fifth was afterwards fixed permanently as the king's rent.

debates: Whether the advice was inspired. Clarke leaves it open between divine inspiration and sound policy; Calvin insists it belongs to the prophetic office itself, which always couples remedy with prediction.
What the fifth part represents. Clarke and Ellicott both take it as a doubling of a customary tenth, justified by the exceptional harvest; Ellicott adds that it later became the permanent royal rent.
Whether Joseph was angling for the post. Gill and Calvin both deny it, Gill from his modesty and his waiting to be asked, Calvin from the fact that the outcome was ordained without his knowledge.
outliers: Ainsworth's translation of the officers as bishops, reported by Clarke, is unlike any other rendering offered.
Gill passes on the Targum's claim that the stored food was to be hidden in a cave in the earth.
themes: gathering against a time of spending
the fifth part and the king's rent
authority as a bridle on plenty

37.pericope_label: Pharaoh recognises the Spirit of God and sets Joseph over his house

schools.summary: Gill records the king's approval of both advice and plan, and observes that any courtier who resented the choice dared not oppose it. Calvin makes necessity the teacher that forced a just appointment where favour usually rules, notes that even a king infatuated by soothsayers may honour the gifts of the Spirit though such knowledge rarely corrects him, keeps the plain sense of kissing in the clause about the people while reading it as a metaphor for cordial obedience, and answers the question whether such pomp befitted a holy man by observing that Joseph could not prescribe his own investiture.

Clarke notes that king and courtiers alike judged the counsel prudent, observes that the words for the Spirit of God are exactly those of the creation account and that Egypt had known the true God long before without ceasing to have gods many, renders the clause about the people from the eastern custom of kissing whatever comes from a superior, and calls the reservation of the throne a perfect description of a prime minister with sole management of the state.

Ellicott ties Pharaoh's verdict back to Joseph's disclaimer, so that the king recognises both the truth of his words and the instrument through whom God spoke, and adds that the wise counsel as much as the interpretation marked him out for the office. He explains the post from the ancient chief of the palace, whose Frankish counterpart ended by taking the crown, canvasses the renderings of the disputed verb and prefers homage to arming or busying, and glosses the reservation as covering all that concerns royal rank and rights.

debates: How the people were to be governed at Joseph's mouth. Ellicott and Clarke keep the sense of kissing and homage; Aben Ezra takes the verb for bearing arms and makes Joseph commander-in-chief; Calvin keeps the word but reads it as metaphor for cordial obedience.

Whether such pomp befitted a holy man. Calvin raises the question and answers that Joseph could not prescribe his own investiture, though God's servants should cut away outward splendour where the choice is theirs.
outliers: Calvin argues that the nobles' failure to contend for the place was a compulsory modesty inspired by fear rather than any real deference.
Ellicott illustrates the power of the office from the Frankish mayors of the palace, who ended by taking the crown outright.
themes: the Spirit of God acknowledged by a heathen king

41.pericope_label: The signet, the linen, the chain, and the procession

schools.summary: Gill recalls that a ring marked admission to the Roman equestrian order and could designate a successor, as Alexander's did for Perdiccas, while denying that Pharaoh meant anything of the kind, and infers from the second chariot only that Joseph stood next to the king and not above him, kings keeping chariots of graduated state.

Clarke makes the signet an office like Lord Keeper of the Privy Seal, cannot settle whether the fine linen was linen or cotton and reports having handled mummy wrappings himself and found them coarse beside Irish linen, reads the gold chain as an emblem of the mutual dependence of king, ministers and people, and declares the herald's cry Egyptian and unknown while offering two Hebrew conjectures.

Ellicott explains the signet as the symbol of legislative power, treats the white linen as the dress of kings and priests and therefore a mark of admission to the ruling class, notes the gold chain among the insignia shown on the monuments, and follows Cook in reading the cry as rejoice, addressed to Joseph by the crowd rather than to the crowd by a herald. Keil and Delitzsch identify the ring as the vizier's seal and derive the cry from a Coptic word for casting down, keeping the sense bow down.

debates: What the herald's cry means. Clarke calls it Egyptian and unknown while offering father-and-tender or father-and-blessing as Hebrew guesses; Keil and Delitzsch derive a Coptic sense of prostration; Ellicott and Cook read it as rejoice, and hold the likeness to the Hebrew for bow the knee accidental.
Who cried it. Keil and Delitzsch assume heralds going before the chariot; Ellicott insists the text makes it the multitude, which is why the word stands in the singular and is addressed to Joseph.
outliers: Clarke reports examining the wrappings of splendid mummies himself and finding them sackcloth beside Irish linen.
Clarke reads the gold chain as a political emblem of the bond between king, ministers and people, defending the method on the ground that antiquity made everything an emblem.
themes: linen as the dress of kings and priests

44.pericope_label: I am Pharaoh: the new name and the marriage at On

schools.summary: Gill takes I am Pharaoh for I am the king, the word being a title rather than a name, and reads it either as reserving the crown or as asserting the authority behind the appointment; on the new name he reports the Targumic and Jewish reading of revealer of secrets while noting that the word occurs nowhere else, that Aben Ezra confessed ignorance of its language, and that some find an Egyptian god's name in its first syllable, as Nebuchadnezzar built one into Daniel's.

Clarke glosses the royal formula the same way, thinks every etymology of the new name doubtful and the Vulgate's rendering arbitrary, and treats the word as an Egyptian title of office; he denies that the priest of On can be Joseph's former master, since this man had children and the other was a eunuch, and takes the closing clause to mean Joseph toured the land to build granaries and appoint officers. Wesley reads the repeated grants as answering opposition at court, and makes the whole preferment a recompense for patient suffering and a type of the exaltation of Christ.

Keil and Delitzsch paraphrase the royal formula as a plain division of rank, prefer a Coptic derivation of the new name yielding sustainer of life, note that name and marriage together were meant to naturalise Joseph, and connect the wife's name with the goddess Neith and her father's with the sun. Ellicott reads the name as food of the living and denies any authority for revealer of secrets, identifies On with the city of the sun and its temple of Ra, and defends the marriage at length from Eastern custom and from Joseph's continued fidelity to the religion of his family.

debates: What the new name means. The Targums and most Jewish writers give revealer of secrets, the Latin tradition saviour of the world, Keil and Delitzsch sustainer of life, and Ellicott food of the living, while Clarke thinks every etymology doubtful and treats it as a bare office title.
Whether Joseph's father-in-law was his former master. Clarke denies it on two grounds, that scripture never hints it and that this man had children.

Whether a worshipper of the one God could rightly marry into an Egyptian priesthood. Ellicott meets the objection from Eastern custom, from the primeval truth still buried in the Egyptian creed, and from the narrative's consistent picture of Joseph's fidelity.
outliers: Gill notes the suggestion that Pharaoh built the name of an Egyptian god into Joseph's new name, as Nebuchadnezzar did when renaming Daniel.
Ellicott adduces an Egyptian story older than Joseph of a foreigner who entered as a herb-seller and ended clothed in kingly attire.
Wesley alone turns the whole preferment into a type of Christ's exaltation, with Joseph as gatherer and disposer of the stores of grace.

46.pericope_label: Joseph at thirty gathers the corn of the plenteous years

schools.summary: Gill dates the thirteen years in Egypt from Joseph's sale at seventeen, glosses the harvest phrase from the reaper's handful and reports the rabbinic and Targumic readings, and insists that only the levied fifth was gathered, bought with the king's money and therefore lawfully resold. Calvin gives two reasons for the recorded age, the singular providence that let a young foreigner govern unenvied and the length of the trial endured, then praises the personal circuit, the prudence of building granaries in every city, the integrity that took nothing for itself, and the diligence that did not slacken though abundance is the mother of idleness.

Henry treats the seven years as a stewardship faithfully kept, Joseph being diligent in laying up while the plenty lasted, and draws the rule that we should foresee the end of the days both of our prosperity and of our opportunity, being neither secure in the one nor slothful in the other, since years of plenty end and we must gather in gathering time.

Clarke works the same arithmetic to thirteen years of slavery and explains that to stand before a sovereign denotes admission to his immediate presence and unlimited confidence, a privilege reserved for the highest favourites. He takes the handfuls to refer principally to rice, which springs in tufts of many stalks from one seed.

Keil and Delitzsch reckon thirteen years as a slave with at least three in prison, render the harvest phrase as full hands or bundles, describe the town granaries holding the produce of the surrounding country, and note that the monuments confirm the practice of measuring corn until the count was abandoned. Ellicott suspects Joseph bought corn beyond the levied fifth while prices were lowest, since the tax also had to cover the running expenses of the realm.

debates: What the earth bringing forth by handfuls describes. Gill reports the reaper's handful and the rabbinic guesses of a stalk full of ears or a grain yielding a handful, with the Targum making it private hoarding; Clarke identifies the crop as rice; Keil and Delitzsch render simply full hands or bundles.
Whether only the tax was stored. Gill holds that the fifth alone was taken, bought with Pharaoh's money; Ellicott thinks Joseph must also have purchased largely at the low prices of those years.
outliers: Clarke's identification of the crop as rice, on the strength of its growing in tufts, stands alone among the voices.
Calvin invokes the proverb that satiety produces disgust to explain why unbroken diligence through seven prosperous years is remarkable.

50.pericope_label: Manasseh and Ephraim born before the famine

schools.summary: Gill notes the singular verb that led one commentator to guess the boys were twins, and takes the dual form of the second name to cover spiritual as well as temporal fruitfulness. Calvin refuses to excuse the forgetting of his father's house: the names breathe genuine piety, but no honour should have displaced that memory, and a viceroy exiled from the Church is still unhappy; he rejects the softer reading that only his brothers' injuries were forgotten, and warns instead against the sweetness of worldly honour, while allowing that Joseph honourably made his sons' names a memorial of his low estate.

Clarke derives both names from their Hebrew verbs and reads them as an acknowledgment that God had let Joseph forget his toil and disgrace and had made him fruitful in the very land of his sufferings. Wesley raises the difficulty without settling it, asking whether Joseph could be so unnatural as to forget his father's house, and observes that Egypt is still called the land of his affliction because distance from his father remained an affliction.

Ellicott defends Joseph outright, taking the phrase to mean that marriage and a child had ended his homesickness and made him contented, so that he no longer pined for the downs of Canaan though his love for his father was undiminished, and adds that the dual ending of the second name intensifies it. Keil and Delitzsch render that name double fruitfulness and find in the words land of my affliction a surviving trace of longing for the promised land.

debates: Whether Joseph sinned in forgetting his father's house. Calvin censures him plainly and refuses the excuses offered; Ellicott holds the phrase means only that his homesickness had ceased; Wesley poses the question and leaves it; Keil and Delitzsch find evidence of continued longing in the other name.
What the dual form of the second name adds. Gill takes it for spiritual and temporal fruitfulness together, Ellicott for simple intensification, Keil and Delitzsch for double fruitfulness.
outliers: Gill passes on the conjecture, drawn from a singular verb, that the two sons were twins.
Calvin observes that men raised from obscurity usually bury their origins, and counts it to Joseph's credit that he made his a permanent memorial.
themes: fruitful in the land of affliction

53.pericope_label: The famine begins and all countries come to buy

schools.summary: Gill dates the change soon after the second birth and describes the river's failure, the parched ground and the seed that would not spring, restrains the phrase about the face of the earth to Egypt itself, and lets the neighbouring nations come gladly for corn; he reports without endorsing the opinion that the Egyptians afterwards worshipped Joseph under their own divine names, and rests instead on his being a type of Christ humbled and exalted. Calvin observes that the good years had already secured Joseph against tumult and that the famine subdued a proud people further, infers from the text that private persons had also stored wheat which would not have lasted, and denies that Pharaoh's referral of the people was indolence rather than confidence.

Clarke attributes the dearth in Egypt to the river reaching only twelve or thirteen cubits while insisting that other causes must explain its spread to countries beyond the Nile, restricts the phrase about the whole earth to that land, and judges that the exacted fifth left little private surplus. He closes with a reflection on a providence general enough to reach every part and particular enough to direct the smallest circumstance, and with a sixfold classification of dreams, warning that there is as much superstition in disregarding them as in heeding them. Wesley notes only that the dearth reached the neighbouring countries as well.

Ellicott explains that before dams and canals regulated the inundation famines were far commoner, argues from the dearth reaching Arabia, Palestine and Ethiopia that the drought was long and general, cites a later Egyptian famine in which a great city was almost emptied of its taxpayers, and reports the argument that Joseph's Pharaoh was the king who first built the system of dykes, locks and reservoirs and the great artificial lake. Keil and Delitzsch trace the inundation itself to rains in the Abyssinian highlands, and describe Joseph opening the granaries and trading corn with Egyptians and foreigners alike.

debates: How far the famine reached. Gill and Clarke hold that the sweeping phrase means the land of Egypt, while allowing that the surrounding nations suffered too; Ellicott names Arabia, Palestine and Ethiopia and infers a long general drought.
Whether private stores existed. Calvin infers from the text that individuals had laid up wheat, though it could not last; Clarke reckons the royal fifth left little beyond ordinary demand.
Why Pharaoh referred the people to Joseph. Calvin rejects the reading that a king was seeking his own ease and makes it a mark of complete confidence.
outliers: Gill reports the belief that the Egyptians afterwards worshipped Joseph under the names of several of their own gods.
Clarke's classification of dreams into six kinds, from bodily disease to direct divine communication, is a set piece unmatched in the chapter.
Ellicott's chronicler records a city falling from three hundred thousand taxpayers to fewer than a hundred souls in a single famine.
